heading: Engineering Trade-offs
subtitle: Not tech opinions — decisions, and the trade-offs accepted with them.

items.title: Kafka vs synchronous communication
items.question: When is an event bus worth the added complexity?
items.answer: When the consumers don't need the update right away, and the producer shouldn't wait on them or depend on their uptime. If the caller needs an answer right now, a direct synchronous call is simpler and easier to follow. But once you need to notify several consumers, replay old events, or scale consumers on their own, an event bus starts to pay off.

items.title: SQL vs NoSQL
items.question: Why default to a relational database?
items.answer: Most business domains have relationships and rules that are worth enforcing at the database level, not just in the application code. I use NoSQL when the data is really document- or key-based, when I need schema flexibility more than strict constraints, or when write scale is the real bottleneck. Not just because it's trendy.

items.title: Monolith vs microservices
items.question: When do microservices actually pay off?
items.answer: When teams need to deploy on their own schedule, or when one part of the system truly needs different scaling or reliability than the rest. Splitting things up before that pressure exists usually just swaps one problem (a large codebase) for a harder one (failures across services) — without a real benefit.

items.title: Cache vs database
items.question: What earns a cache instead of just hitting the database?
items.answer: Read-heavy paths where speed matters and the data can be a little out of date. The trade-off is always the extra work of keeping the cache in sync. So I only add one once I can point to the exact query or endpoint that needs it, with a clear plan for when to refresh it.

items.title: Consistency vs availability
items.question: How do you decide where a system sits on that spectrum?
items.answer: I ask what a stale or failed read actually costs in that specific case. A financial transaction should favor consistency, even if that means going down during a network split. A product catalog should favor availability — a slightly outdated price is a smaller problem than the whole page failing to load.

items.title: REST vs event-driven
items.question: How do you choose between a request/response API and an event-driven flow?
items.answer: REST when a client needs a direct answer to a specific question. Event-driven when the goal is to tell several independent consumers that something happened, without the producer needing to know who's listening. Most systems end up using both, side by side, rather than picking just one.
